chef_bio.background: 「豚ノヴァ 零-zero- 神田水道橋店」は、国分寺で人気の二郎系ラーメン店「豚NOVA（豚ノヴァ）」の2号店として、JR水道橋駅・神保町駅の間、水道橋駅東口徒歩5分の場所に2025年3月8日にグランドオープンした。 国分寺本店とは異なり、通常のラーメンは提供せず「汁なし（マゼソバ寄りの二郎インスパイア）」専門の一杯に特化している。 店主のGo氏は埼玉の人気二郎系店「富士丸 東浦和店」や「D麺」で修行した経歴を持つ。
chef_bio.philosophy: 経営上の数字よりも味への一切の妥協のなさを優先しており、一杯あたりの原価率は60%を超えるという。 国分寺本店の味をベースにしながら、カエシ・豚・トッピングを細かく調整し、神田水道橋店ならではの独自の味わいに仕上げている。
chef_bio.specialty: 汁なし（二郎インスパイア系の油そば・まぜそば）。 丼全体を混ぜると小麦の甘みを含んだ香りが立ち上る、汁なし専用に配合・形状を変えた自家製麺が看板。

anecdotes.text: 汁なし専用の麺は、汁なしのために小麦の配合や形状を変えたもので、丼全体をかき混ぜた時に小麦の甘みを含んだ香りがフワッと立ち上り、ムチっとした食感に密度の高い小麦感が味わえます。二郎系の名店で修行をしたGo店主が作り上げた、こだわりの麺です。
豚ノヴァは、経営的な数値を度外視して味に対して一切の妥協なく提供をしており、一杯の原価率は60%を超えており、これは最高の原材料で最高の味を提供するためです。
店主は埼玉の人気二郎系店「富士丸 東浦和店」と「D麺」で修行した。
2025年3月8日、国分寺に続く2号店として神田水道橋にグランドオープンした（水道橋駅徒歩5分）。

Press coverage describes it as a deliberately low-key 'hideaway' offering an escape from the tourist bustle around the temple.
chef_bio.philosophy: The brand states it wants to honor the spirit of traditional tea ceremony and the beauty of matcha while reinterpreting it, not as something formal, but in a form that fits naturally into modern daily life.
chef_bio.specialty: Build-your-own matcha latte — customers choose the matcha grade, intensity, sweetness, milk, flavor (options include kuromitsu, kinako, houjicha, melon, mango, strawberry, chocolate, yuzu) and toppings (warabimochi, anko, cream); also known for its handmade 'demekin taiyaki' filled with matcha custard.

anecdotes.text: MATCHA TIMES sources its matcha directly from five long-established manufacturers, each with over 100 years of history, to ensure high, consistent quality across its customizable drink menu.
The Asakusa shop was deliberately sited away from the main tourist strip near Kaminarimon, on a quiet residential street up a flight of stairs, to create a calmer 'hideaway' matcha experience.

positives.text: Core matcha lattes are built from matcha powder, milk, and naturally gluten-free flavor add-ins like kuromitsu, kinako, and houjicha, with no dashi or soy-sauce-based savory dishes on the menu to introduce hidden wheat or fish stock.

source_independence.note: This source reprints shop marketing rather than reporting a visit (a curated hub or a press release). It corroborates that a claim was MADE, not that it was verified.

cultural_comfort.note: Ordering is menu-and-counter style with a build-your-own matcha system (grade, strength, sweetness, milk, flavor, toppings); an English-speaking visitor can point at menu boards but detailed customization is explained mostly in Japanese.

chef_bio.background: Shinjuku Soba Kura (信州そば処 新宿そば蔵) is the Shinjuku Sanchome branch of Sobakura, a small two-shop Shinshu (Nagano)-style soba group that also runs a location in Komazawa. chef_bio.philosophy: The group's stated aim, per its official site, is '本場信州のそばを味わう喜び' — the joy of tasting authentic Shinshu soba — built around buckwheat noodles and sake sourced fresh from Nagano every day.
chef_bio.specialty: 錦そば (Nishiki Soba), plus shiso (青じそ) flavored variations and Shinshu-style mori soba

anecdotes.text: The shop is run day-to-day by two women in a small counter-and-table space (about 12 seats) with a casual, nostalgic standing-soba-shop atmosphere; regulars praise the firm, fresh-tasting Nagano buckwheat noodles and the crisp vegetable and shrimp tempura, alongside snacks like nozawana pickles and horse sashimi (basashi) to go with the local sake.
Weekday moriSoba runs around ¥550 and a half-rice teishoku set around ¥935, reflecting the shop's casual, affordable pricing.

cultural_comfort.note: A small, casual, locally-run soba stand with no confirmed English menu or English-speaking staff; some Japanese ability (or pointing at the tabelog/menu photos) will help when ordering.

tokyo_kamiyama.gf_detail: This is a traditional Edo-style soba-ya, not a gluten-free-focused kitchen. Some descriptions reference stone-ground buckwheat prepared fresh daily, but there is no confirmation the noodles are consistently 十割 (100% buckwheat, wheat-free) rather than the common 二八 blend (buckwheat plus wheat flour as binder), and the dipping sauce/dashi (tsuyu) follows the standard soy-sauce-and-bonito-dashi style typical of old-line soba shops, which normally contains wheat. Tempura is also on the menu, fried in shared oil with a wheat-flour batter. No gluten-free protocol, dedicated fryer, or wheat-free soy sauce was mentioned in any available source, so celiac or strictly gluten-free diners should not assume safety here without calling ahead and asking directly.
tokyo_kamiyama.vegan_detail: This is a classic soba-ya built around bonito (katsuo) dashi, with tempura and sashimi also on the menu, so it is not vegan-oriented. Even a plain zaru soba would typically be served with a bonito-based dipping sauce. No plant-based dashi or vegan menu option was found in any source reviewed.

Buckwheat is stone-ground on site each morning and mixed with spring water said to be drawn from the Haruna mountain area, used for both the noodles and the dashi.

positives.text: Uses domestically grown buckwheat, stone-ground on the premises each morning for freshly milled noodles.

gf_cross_contamination.text: The salad-bar dressing is described as a miso-type dressing (with salt, olive oil, vinegar); miso is frequently produced with barley (mugi) or wheat koji, i.e. a hidden gluten source on the shared bar that no GF claim addresses.

tokyo_teuchi_soba_ozawa.gf_detail: This is a traditional hand-cut soba-ya, not a gluten-free-focused establishment. Of its three noodle cuts, the medium ('yaya futomen') noodle is reportedly made juwari-style (十割, 100% buckwheat flour with no wheat binder), while the thin noodle uses roughly 90% buckwheat/10% wheat and the ultra-thick noodle about 95% buckwheat/5% wheat -- so two of the three cuts do contain some wheat flour. No source confirms dedicated gluten-free boiling water, separate prep equipment, or a wheat-free dipping sauce; standard soba tsuyu is soy-sauce (shoyu) based and typically contains wheat. Diners with celiac disease should not assume any cut is safe without asking staff directly, given the shared kitchen and likely shared boiling water across noodle types.
tokyo_teuchi_soba_ozawa.vegan_detail: No vegan-specific menu, labeling, or accommodation was found for this shop. As a traditional soba-ya, its dipping sauce (tsuyu) almost certainly rests on a katsuobushi (bonito) dashi with a soy-sauce-based kaeshi, which is standard practice for hand-cut soba shops of this type and is not vegan. No source confirms a kombu-only or vegetable-broth alternative.
tokyo_teuchi_soba_ozawa.notes: [Mom & Pop] This is a traditional hand-cut soba-ya, not a gluten-free-focused establishment. Of its three noodle cuts, the medium ('yaya futomen') noodle is reportedly made juwari-style (十割, 100% buckwheat flour with no wheat binder), while the thin noodle uses roughly 90% buckwheat/10% whea · 📍 Approx. map location — confirm the exact spot (auto-placed from address).

chef_bio.philosophy: The shop varies the ratio of buckwheat to wheat binder to match each cut's texture: roughly 90% buckwheat for the thin noodle (smoother throat-feel), a 100%-buckwheat (juwari) blend for the medium noodle, and about 95% buckwheat for the ultra-thick noodle, using buckwheat flour sourced from various regions of Japan.
chef_bio.specialty: Three hand-cut soba noodle styles served side by side: a thin 'tsurutsuru hosogiri' (smooth, easy-swallowing thin cut), a nutty 'mochimochi arabiki' (coarse-ground cut), and an ultra-thick 'mogumogu futoi' (太打ち) noodle roughly 1cm wide, marketed as among the thickest hand-cut soba in Tokyo -- cut so wide that a single serving can contain as few as about 8 strands.

anecdotes.text: The 太打ち (ultra-thick) noodle is cut so wide that a single serving of soba contains only around 8 strands -- an oddity that has made it a minor food-blog phenomenon in Asakusa, often described as 'Japan's thickest soba'.

cultural_comfort.note: A small, traditional neighborhood soba-ya with no confirmed English menu or online reservation system -- some basic Japanese (or pointing at the Tabelog photos) will help when ordering.

Not recommended for celiac diners.

chef_bio.background: Fupao Sakaba (福包酒場) is a casual offshoot of the same operators' upscale restaurant, 中国家庭料理 香園 (Chinese home cooking restaurant Kōen); the brand was created to bring the same dim-sum techniques and recipes to a lower price point. It has since grown into a multi-location Chinese-izakaya chain with branches across Tokyo (Roppongi, Shibuya, Ikebukuro), Kanagawa, Osaka, Sendai and other cities, and is actively recruiting franchisees. This Shibuya branch sits in the middle of Shibuya Chuo-gai on Dogenzaka, about a 2-minute walk from Shibuya Station's south exit / Inokashira Line west exit.
chef_bio.philosophy: The restaurant describes itself as committed to its ingredients, cooking methods, dining space and hospitality ("食材や調理法、空間から接客まで、お客様をおもてなしすることにこだわっています"), aiming to entertain guests visually as well as through flavor.
chef_bio.specialty: 5-color soup dumplings (5色小籠包) — five hand-made xiaolongbao, each wrapped in a differently colored, differently flavored skin, served in a bamboo steamer that releases a cloud of steam when opened; listed as the shop's most popular item, especially with women.

anecdotes.text: Monday–Friday 4–6pm the restaurant runs a 60-minute all-you-can-drink deal on sour cocktails for 1 yen, letting guests choose two flavors from the menu.
The five-color xiaolongbao are prized as much for the burst of steam and color when the steamer basket is opened as for their flavor, making them a popular photo moment.

cultural_comfort.note: No confirmed English menu or English-speaking staff; ordering by pointing at photos or basic Japanese should be sufficient at this casual izakaya.

tokyo_meidai_shiraki_soba.gf_detail: No gluten-free noodle, sauce, or accommodation is advertised anywhere. This is a conventional soba counter using standard (wheat-buckwheat blend, not 十割/juwari) noodles, and its signature dipping sauce (tsuyu) is soy-sauce-based, which in Japan is almost always wheat-containing — not appropriate for celiac-level gluten-free needs. chef_bio.specialty: Gyuniku (beef) tsukesoba — thick, firm soba noodles served alongside a rich, chili-oil-spiked dipping broth topped with simmered beef; other versions include nori, grated yam (tororo), and duck.

anecdotes.text: The shop shifted from a generic stand-up soba counter to a dedicated tsukesoba specialist focused on hearty beef soba made with deliberately hard, thick noodles.
Featured as a weekday lunch pick for the Hongo/Suidobashi office-worker crowd, ordered via a ticket vending machine at the counter.

cultural_comfort.note: Ordering is via a Japanese-language ticket vending machine at the counter (PayPay QR accepted as an alternative), with no indication of an English menu — comfortable for diners with basic Japanese or point-and-order confidence.

tokyo_juwari_soba_sagatani_shi_2.gf_detail: The soba noodles are 100% buckwheat (juwari) with no wheat flour used as a binder, which is unusual for soba (most soba blends in wheat flour) and a genuine plus for wheat-avoidant diners. However, the tsuyu dipping sauce is a standard Japanese preparation and Japanese soy sauce is normally brewed with wheat as well as soybeans, so the sauce very likely contains wheat; tempura toppings use ordinary wheat-flour batter and are fried in what is likely a shared fryer. No dedicated gluten-free menu, ingredient list, or allergen protocol for this location was found, so this cannot be confirmed safe for celiac disease — order plain soba and ask staff about the sauce and frying oil if strict avoidance is required.
tokyo_juwari_soba_sagatani_shi_2.vegan_detail: Not vegan-focused: the standard tsuyu/broth for both hot and cold soba is made with kombu and bonito (katsuobushi) dashi, so the default dipping sauce and hot soup contain fish. No plant-based dashi or dedicated vegan menu was found for this location. The soba noodles themselves are just buckwheat and water (no egg), but they are normally served with the fish-based sauce/broth, and tempura batter/toppings are not confirmed vegan either.

chef_bio.background: Sagatani was launched in Tokyo in 2011 by operator For You Co. , Ltd. (株式会社フォーユー) to bring authentic 100%-buckwheat 'juwari' soba — normally the domain of pricier specialty soba-ya — into the cheap, fast tachigui (stand-and-eat) soba format. The chain grew to roughly 8-9 locations across central Tokyo. This Shinjuku Keio Mall branch sits underground in the Keio Mall shopping arcade just off Shinjuku Station's west exit and opened in December 2021.
chef_bio.philosophy: The chain's motto is '挽きたて・打ちたて・茹でたて・揚げたて' (freshly milled, freshly made, freshly boiled, freshly fried): buckwheat is stone-ground on site and the flour's water content is adjusted daily to match the weather and season, aiming to deliver specialty-shop soba quality at stand-and-eat prices and speed.
chef_bio.specialty: 十割そば (juwari soba) — noodles made from 100% buckwheat flour with no wheat used as a binder, milled fresh in-house each day on an in-store electric stone mill.

anecdotes.text: Another reviewer calls it their 'go-to spot when the weather turns cold' (寒くなった時の定番), describing it as a reliable, comforting choice near the station.

gf_cross_contamination.text: Restaurants in most cases boil udon and soba in the same large pot (same water), so cross-contamination via the boiling water requires caution; and restaurant menus have no obligation to display allergens.

Many restaurants share frying oil for tempura, tonkatsu and other fried foods; Sagatani's tempura is described by a user as low-quality (soba is the flagship, tempura is cost-cut) — indicating no dedicated GF frying setup.

GF blog promoting Sagatani frames it as gluten-free for people doing GF 'for daily performance and health,' and notes tempura/tempura flakes contain gluten and regular soy sauce is brewed with wheat — i.e., strict-GF diners should avoid those — which is lifestyle-GF framing, not a celiac-safety guarantee.

Search-surfaced FindMeGlutenFree text ('ask for gluten free menu... they change the flour to rice for frying... gluten-free soy sauce available') does not clearly attribute these accommodations to the Shinjuku Keio Mall branch and appears conflated across Sagatani/Shibuya locations; unverifiable and single-source.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Standard Japanese soy sauce (shoyu), the base of soba tsuyu, is typically brewed from wheat and soybeans together — this is general Japanese food-labeling guidance, not a statement specific to this shop's own recipe, but it applies to conventional tsuyu of the kind this chain serves.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The chain's broth is described as made with kombu and a blend of dried bonito (katsuobushi) stocks for both the cold and hot tsuyu, meaning the soup base is fish-derived and not vegan.

positives.text: Noodles are 100% buckwheat (juwari) with no wheat used as a binder, milled fresh in-store daily on an electric stone mill — a genuine plus versus ordinary soba, which typically blends in wheat flour.

cultural_comfort.note: Ordering is via a Japanese-language ticket vending machine (食券制) — cash or transit IC card — typical of fast soba counters, so a little Japanese or willingness to point at machine buttons/photos helps.

chef_bio.background: Menya Musashi (麺屋武蔵) is a Tokyo ramen company founded in 1996 in Aoyama by Yamada Yuu, part of the influential wave of "1996-generation" Tokyo ramen shops credited with reshaping the genre. Bukotsu Gaiden ("the rugged sequel") is one of the company's Shibuya spin-off/sister brands, opened in the mid-2000s a short walk from Shibuya Station, and it has become one of the busiest tsukemen (dipping noodle) specialists in the neighborhood, known for very generous, freely-refillable noodle portions.
chef_bio.philosophy: Menya Musashi's founding concept was to run a ramen shop with the warmth and hospitality of a good izakaya, on the belief that the whole dining experience — not just the taste of the broth — is what makes a bowl of ramen genuinely satisfying.
chef_bio.specialty: Noukou Gaiden Kuro Tsukemen (rich black dipping noodles) — thick, chewy noodles served cold alongside a choice of three dipping broths: black (finished with a special soy-based tare), red (finished with a spicy miso paste), and plain white (no added paste), each available in a standard or richer katsuobushi-enhanced version.

anecdotes.text: The shop offers three colors of dipping sauce — white, black, and red — each built on a shared chicken-and-pork-bone base with dried sardine and bonito, letting diners compare three distinct flavor profiles in one visit.
A regular customer described it as the reward at the end of a long workday, praising the volume of noodles (up to 1kg free) and the richness of the black dipping broth topped with a soft-boiled egg.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: The black-style dipping broth is finished with a special soy-sauce-based tare (paste), a wheat-containing seasoning typical of shoyu-style ramen.

cultural_comfort.note: Counter-only seating with a Japanese-language ticket machine and no reservations; the three broth colors (white/black/red) are easy to identify visually even without fluent Japanese, but ordering noodle amount/toppings may require pointing or basic phrases.

tokyo_raamen_hayashida_shinjuk.gf_detail: This is a standard wheat-noodle ramen shop: the noodles are wheat-based and the tare/seasoning for both the shoyu and shio versions relies on soy sauce, which typically contains wheat. No vegetarian or vegan broth alternative, plant-based noodle, or meat-free menu item was found in any source, and additional non-vegan ingredients (e.g., chashu pork/chicken) are standard toppings. Not suitable for vegan or vegetarian diners.

chef_bio.background: Hayashida built its name on a clear, richly flavored chicken "seiyu" (clear consommé-style) broth. Whole chicken and duck are simmered from early morning for hours, with the cooks carefully skimming off scum (aku) so the finished soup stays clean and translucent rather than cloudy.
chef_bio.philosophy: The kitchen centers the bowl on pure chicken umami, using duck to add a rounder, sweeter backbone to the broth, then balances that roundness with a crisp, well-defined tare (seasoning sauce) so the soup doesn't taste flat.
chef_bio.specialty: Tokusei shoyu ramen (特製醤油らぁ麺) — a soy-sauce ramen built on the shop's signature clear chicken-and-duck broth, served alongside a salt (shio) version and tsukemen.

anecdotes.text: Duck and whole chicken are used generously from early morning and simmered for a long time, with the cooks skimming the scum thoroughly to produce a highly refined, clear soup.

tokyo_vegan_izakaya_masaka.gf_detail: No dedicated gluten-free menu or wheat-free certification was found. The restaurant is listed on WE TABLE, a Tokyo directory of allergy-conscious dining spots, suggesting some willingness to discuss allergens, but no specific celiac-safety statement (dedicated fryer, wheat-free tamari, etc.) was confirmed. tokyo_vegan_izakaya_masaka.vegan_detail: Fully plant-based menu (20+ dishes always available) — soy-meat karaage, vegan gyoza, and other classic izakaya small plates, all made without meat, fish, dairy, or eggs. As a 100%-vegan kitchen there is no hidden dashi/katsuobushi (bonito) risk from the standard menu.

chef_bio.background: Run by Bird Feather Nobu Co. (株式会社バードフェザーノブ), the shop set out to recreate a classic, everyday Japanese izakaya — complete with a Showa-retro noren curtain entrance — using only plant-based ingredients throughout the kitchen.
chef_bio.philosophy: The team wants vegan food to feel like normal, affordable izakaya fare rather than a special or expensive category, so that vegan and non-vegan customers can sit down and eat the same dishes together. In interviews the shop describes wanting to subvert the assumption that vegan cooking is difficult or costly to access, and to patiently walk first-time or unfamiliar customers through what 'vegan' actually means on the menu.
chef_bio.specialty: Soy-meat karaage (plant-based 'fried chicken') — crispy outside and moist inside — served with a choice of about seven sauces, alongside vegan gyoza and lemon sours.

anecdotes.text: The restaurant keeps a retro Showa-era izakaya look with a noren curtain entrance, and draws daily interest from both regular Japanese customers and international visitors curious about vegan food.

Staff are described as taking care to walk unfamiliar or skeptical customers through the menu, addressing the common feeling that vegan food is 'unfamiliar' or 'looks difficult,' rather than assuming everyone already understands veganism.
The shop's stated goal is to 'subvert expectations in a good way,' building an izakaya where vegans and non-vegans can enjoy the same affordable, everyday dishes together.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Every dish on the menu is made using only plant-derived ingredients — the kitchen does not use meat, fish, dairy, or eggs at all, which removes the risk of animal-product cross-contact that vegan diners would face in a mixed kitchen.

positives.text: The restaurant is listed on WE TABLE, a Tokyo guide specifically curating restaurants that accommodate food allergies and special diets.
Also listed on Vegewel, a dedicated vegetarian/vegan/gluten-free restaurant directory for Japan.

cultural_comfort.note: It sits inside the very tourist-heavy Shibuya PARCO complex and multiple write-ups mention international visitors dining here, but no confirmed English-language menu was found, so basic Japanese/pointing may still be needed.

tokyo_marugo_s.gf_detail: No gluten-free menu, wheat-free labeling, or allergen chart was found in the official site, opening press release, or blog reviews checked. anecdotes.text: A blog reviewer described MARUGO S as a hidden-gem seating option inside the often fully-booked FOOD STADIUM TOKYO food hall, noting the three-way curry combo's flavor is approachable and not aggressively spiced, making it easy to eat.

The shop is also known for a delicate 'snow' dessert — yogurt-based shaved ice with fresh berries, pistachio sauce, and espuma — that reportedly must be eaten within about five minutes before it melts.

cultural_comfort.note: Ordering and menu appear Japanese-only in available sources; however it sits inside Tokyo Dome City's food hall, a major tourist-trafficked complex, so staff are likely used to some non-Japanese-speaking visitors even though this isn't confirmed.

chef_bio.background: Oda Akinobu, a Kyoto-born (1967) former music-magazine editor and international touring/artist-booking coordinator, opened Nagi Shokudo in December 2007 in Shibuya's quiet Uguisudani-cho backstreet. He later authored several books about the shop, including "渋谷のすみっこでベジ食堂" ("A Veg Diner in a Corner of Shibuya") and vegetable-recipe collections.
chef_bio.philosophy: Oda noticed that many of the touring overseas musicians he booked and worked with were vegetarian, and that Japan had very few vegetarian/vegan restaurants with bold, rice- and drink-friendly flavors. He set out to create a place serving hearty, flavorful all-vegan food where music-scene friends could also gather casually, like a friend's living room.
chef_bio.specialty: なぎAセット (Nagi A-Set): soft-cooked brown rice, miso soup, soy-meat karaage (fried soy-meat 'chicken'), and a rotating daily vegetable side — the restaurant's signature set meal (about ¥1,100). Lunch offers a choice of 3 from roughly 14 rotating vegetable side dishes.

anecdotes.text: Oda opened the restaurant after realizing, through his work booking international touring artists (many of whom were vegetarian), that Japan lacked vegetarian restaurants serving richly flavored food that pairs well with rice and alcohol — and wanted a spot where his music-industry friends could also gather.

The dining room has a lived-in, 'friend's house' atmosphere with indie rock playing, table seating plus a small raised tatami-style nook, and draws a mixed crowd of women, older men, Japanese residents, and foreign tourists/expats alike.

chef_bio.background: Tokyo Sundubu (東京純豆腐) is a Korean soft-tofu-stew (sundubu jjigae) specialty chain run by Beans One Company. According to the company's own history page, the founders fell for sundubu while in New York and wanted Japanese diners to feel that same excitement, which led to the brand's launch in 2006 — the first four shops, opened that year, included Aoyama, Shibuya, Azabudai and this Shinjuku location. The company describes its goal as making sundubu into a household 'national dish' in Japan and, as of 2026, marks 20 years as (by its own account) the largest sundubu-specialty chain in the country.
chef_bio.philosophy: In-house, daily-made tofu from domestic soybeans, paired with a long-simmered broth (beef-bone base with seafood and vegetables, gochujang-seasoned) that the company markets as its point of pride ('だしにこだわったスープ').
chef_bio.specialty: Made-to-order sundubu jjigae (soft tofu stew): diners choose a soup base (salt, miso, or white), a spice level (1-6), and rice portion. Tofu is made fresh in-house daily from domestic soybeans and served at the soft, just-set stage before it fully firms.

anecdotes.text: The founders discovered sundubu while in New York and wanted to bring that same excitement back to Japan, which is what led to Tokyo Sundubu's 2006 launch, with this Shinjuku shop among the brand's first locations.

gf_cross_contamination.text: The standard sundubu broth used chain-wide contains clams, fried tofu (abura-age), egg, and shellfish extract, and is prepared in a shared kitchen alongside meat and seafood dishes, so cross-contact with wheat/gluten-containing ingredients is likely.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: Chain-wide allergen listings for the soup include wheat (小麦), soy, and sesame among the ingredients used in the gochujang-based broth.

vegan_cross_contact.text: All standard sundubu broths include clams, egg, and shellfish extract as base ingredients, so the shared broth is not suitable for vegan diners and cross-contact with animal products is inherent to the standard menu.

staff_allergy_handling.text: At least one Tokyo Sundubu branch (Ikebukuro) keeps a printed allergy/ingredient chart near the entrance/register that staff can check with guests on request; this practice is not separately confirmed for the Shinjuku branch.

positives.text: Diners can customize spice level (1-6), soup type, and rice portion at order time, which gives some control over what goes into the bowl even though the base broth itself is fixed.

cultural_comfort.note: Ordering is simple (pick soup type, spice level 1-6, and rice amount) and the chain has an English-language Tabelog listing, but in-store menus and staff communication are primarily in Japanese, so basic Japanese or pointing/apps will help.

chef_bio.origin: Part of the "Uogashi Nihon-ichi" chain run by Nippan Co. — Japan's pioneering standing-sushi (tachigui-zushi) concept, whose flagship store opened near Shimbashi Station on June 19, 1989.
chef_bio.background: Uogashi Nihon-ichi popularized the idea of hand-pressed Edomae sushi served fast, at a standing counter, for working commuters — a deliberate throwback to the roadside sushi stalls (sushi yatai) of Edo-period Tokyo roughly 200 years earlier. The Shibuya Dogenzaka branch is one of many locations across the chain, sourcing fish daily from markets stretching from Hokkaido in the north to Kyushu in the south.
chef_bio.philosophy: The chain's guiding principle since its founding is "nana-tate" (七たて) — seven kinds of freshness: freshly caught, freshly filleted, freshly simmered, freshly grilled, freshly fried, freshly cooked rice, and freshly hand-pressed. The idea is to serve quality, reasonably priced ingredients simply — cold food served cold, hot food served hot.
chef_bio.specialty: Hand-pressed nigiri sushi made to order at the standing counter, priced individually by piece so diners can eat as much or as little as they like.

anecdotes.text: The chain's June 19, 1989 opening date at its original Shimbashi store is commemorated on Japanese trivia calendars as related to the standing-sushi format's debut.

cultural_comfort.note: An English-language menu and point-and-order style make it workable for non-Japanese speakers, but the fast-paced standing-counter format and staff interactions are primarily in Japanese.

chef_bio.background: A hushed, Shōwa-era kissaten reached by a stairway down into a basement near Shinjuku's east side, open since 1985. The dim, quiet room has individually partitioned counter seats so solo customers can sit undisturbed with their coffee, and shelves lined with roughly 1,500 antique cups and saucers from makers like Wedgwood, Meissen, Ginori and Royal Copenhagen — each order is served in a different cup, with a card explaining that day's maker.

anecdotes.text: Because the shortcake is capped at 16 pieces a day and only appears when the strawberries are good, regulars call it the 'phantom shortcake' (幻のショートケーキ).

chef_bio.background: NEW YORKER'S Cafe is a self-service espresso cafe brand created by Ginza Renoir, the long-running Japanese kissaten (traditional coffee shop) company. When Ginza Renoir hit a business downturn during Japan's deflationary period, management converted one of its underperforming full-service Takadanobaba locations into a self-service, New York-style espresso bar as an experiment. The revamped shop drew a completely new customer base of women and students who had never visited the original waiter-service Renoir cafes, and sales roughly tripled, leading the company to roll the concept out to additional locations including this Suidobashi east-exit branch.
chef_bio.philosophy: Branded around the concept of "My Style Cafe" and a space designed to feel like "a New York-inspired oasis in the city," the cafe aims to let each guest use the space in their own way — for coffee alone, a quick meal, work, or study — in a stylish, espresso-bar-style setting distinct from its parent chain's traditional waiter-service kissaten.
chef_bio.specialty: Hand-poured espresso and coffee drinks alongside bread-based light meals such as salmon and cream cheese bagels, prosciutto and camembert focaccia, and roast chicken and cheddar focaccia, plus multiple breakfast sets (soup, bagel, hot dog, focaccia or buttered toast, each with a mini salad).

anecdotes.text: The NEW YORKER'S Cafe concept began as a make-or-break experiment: Ginza Renoir converted a money-losing, waiter-service Takadanobaba shop into a self-service espresso cafe, and it ended up tripling sales by attracting younger and female customers the original brand had not reached.

anecdotes.text: The restaurant developed its own original gin, "Torinosu Shibuya Remix," in collaboration with a sake brewery in Kagoshima, served alongside a natural wine list to pair with the grilled chicken courses.

chef_bio.background: Hikiniku to Come was founded in 2019 by restaurateur Yamamoto Shohei (previously behind the hamburger chain "Ore no Hamburg") together with Konishi Toshiyuki of the design firm POOL inc. and Kiyomiya Toshiyuki, a food-service veteran who had worked at Culture Convenience Club (TSUTAYA) and Chikara no Moto Holdings (Ippudo ramen). The first shop opened in Kichijoji in June 2020, and the concept quickly grew into a multi-location chain; the Shibuya branch on Dogenzaka opened in March 2021 inside a renovated older building, giving it a hidden, back-alley feel despite the crowds it draws.
chef_bio.philosophy: The restaurant is built around a "3-fresh" (3たて) idea — meat ground fresh, patties grilled fresh over charcoal, and rice cooked fresh to order — reflecting founder Yamamoto Shohei's belief that ground meat deserves to be the star of the dish rather than just a component of a burger or curry.
chef_bio.specialty: 挽肉と米定食 — a single set meal of freshly ground, charcoal-grilled beef hamburger-steak patties (up to three 90g patties), rice cooked fresh in kamado pots, and miso soup, with free rice refills and a complimentary raw egg. The Shibuya location also has its own house sauce blended from three types of miso.

anecdotes.text: Yamamoto Shohei's path to Hikiniku to Come ran through his earlier venture "Ore no Hamburg," and he has spoken about why he became fixated specifically on ground meat (挽肉) as a craft rather than treating it as a secondary ingredient.

Since opening in 2021, the Shibuya branch has been known for long same-day queues, moving from a paper numbered-ticket (整理券) system to a mix of same-day sign-up and limited paid online reservations for a small 6-seat counter area.

cultural_comfort.note: The menu is a single set meal so ordering itself is simple even without Japanese, but the entry process (same-day sign-up/queue system, occasional online reservation windows) is explained mainly in Japanese and can be confusing for first-time foreign visitors.

chef_bio.philosophy: Preserving the traditional taste the restaurant has served since 1962 while incorporating contemporary menu elements and ingredients.

chef_bio.background: Opened in 1947 (Shōwa 22), just after the end of World War II, in the Asakusa Kannon-ura district directly behind Sensō-ji Temple. The founding family had previously run a sake retail business before turning the shop into a dedicated beef-tendon-stew specialist. It has been passed down through the family and is now counted among the oldest surviving izakaya in the Kannon-ura backstreets.
chef_bio.philosophy: The recipe has been kept deliberately unchanged since the shop opened. Beef tendon — sourced from Hiyama, a long-established wholesaler in Nihonbashi — is simmered for hours in a broth built up over decades, preserving the same flavor generation to generation.
chef_bio.specialty: Gyusuji nikomi (牛すじ煮込み) — Asakusa-style beef tendon stew, the dish the shop was founded on and has served continuously since 1947.

anecdotes.text: The current proprietress has said that her father passed away ten years ago, and if he woke up and tasted today's beef tendon stew, he might still say 'this is a bit too sweet' — a sign of how carefully the original recipe is still followed.
The beef tendon is simmered for roughly four hours a day using tendon from Hiyama, a century-old Nihonbashi meat wholesaler, continuing a broth-and-technique tradition built up over decades.

cultural_comfort.note: A traditional, regulars-heavy local izakaya with no confirmed English menu, though it has appeared on Japanese TV programs and is listed in English on Tabelog.

chef_bio.background: REC COFFEE was founded in Fukuoka in 2008 by Yoshikazu Iwase and his university friend and business partner Osamu Kitazoe, starting as a mobile coffee truck before opening its first storefront near Yakuin Station in 2010. Iwase discovered specialty coffee while working part-time at Manu Coffee in Fukuoka under roaster Sonobu Nishioka, which shaped his approach to sourcing and roasting. The company grew from Fukuoka into multiple Tokyo locations (including this Suidobashi shop, on the ground floor of the Nine Hours Suidobashi capsule hotel building by the Kandagawa river) and into Taiwan.
chef_bio.philosophy: Iwase has said his goal is to serve coffee good enough to change how everyday consumers think about coffee, treating quality specialty coffee as something for daily life rather than a niche connoisseur product.
chef_bio.specialty: Single-origin, self-roasted specialty pour-over and espresso coffee, paired with house-made pastries (honey financiers, almond sables, pound cakes) baked by an in-house pastry team.

anecdotes.text: Iwase won Japan's national barista championship (JBC) in both 2014 and 2015, then took silver at the 2016 World Barista Championship in Dublin, Ireland -- accolades that grew out of the roasting and brewing standards set at the original Fukuoka shop.

Iwase has described wanting to bring specialty coffee into Fukuoka's cafe culture in a way that changes ordinary consumers' image of what coffee can taste like, rather than keeping it a specialist pursuit.

chef_bio.background: Tsunahachi traces back to 1922, when founder Kyuzo Shimura opened a stand-and-eat tempura shop called "Amihachi" (網八). Customers habitually misread the character 網 (ami) as tsuna, and the mispronunciation stuck so firmly that in 1924 the shop was formally reopened under the name it kept the same location in Shinjuku's old Tsunohazu district as today's Sohonten. The original building was destroyed in the 1945 air raids and post-war land readjustment; the shop rebuilt and reopened on the same ground in 1948. Over nine decades the company grew into one of Japan's best-known tempura chains, with roughly 23 branches nationwide (Sapporo, Toyama, Nagoya, Kyoto, Osaka and more) as of early 2026. In 2026 the flagship Sohonten building closed for a full rebuild planned to run until summer 2028; during construction the original staff and craftsmen relocated a minute's walk away to a temporary location, 'Sohonten Bekkan' (総本店別館), inside the TRES SHINJUKU building, which opened June 23, 2026.
chef_bio.philosophy: The house motto, carried since the founder's era, is to 'always serve the finest tempura at an accessible price' and to 'add sincerity to every dish' (常に最高の天ぷらをお手頃な価格で / おいしさに真心をそえて).

chef_bio.origin: Founded in 1961 (Shōwa 36) in Nerima Ward's Tagashira, the shop later moved to Nakano, then to Shinjuku's Shokuan-dōri, before settling at its current West Shinjuku location behind Bic Camera, near Shinjuku Station's west exit.
chef_bio.specialty: Chāshū Zaru — a cold dipping-noodle (tsukemen) bowl piled with seven or more slices of pork char siu, each over a centimeter thick, served alongside a tangy, savory soy-based dipping broth and thick, chewy curly noodles.

anecdotes.text: The shop's founder, referred to as Mr. Takano, is described as the figure whose ramen and career later became the root of the well-known 'Horiuchi' shōyū-ramen family tree in Shinjuku, after moves through Nerima and Nakano before landing at the current West Shinjuku spot.

Reviewers repeatedly describe the chāshū zaru as burying the bowl in meat — thick-cut pork slices covering the noodles almost entirely — a signature so consistent that customers say the taste 'hasn't changed' across decades of visits.

cultural_comfort.note: Ordering is via a cash-only ticket machine with a short, simple menu (ramen or tsukemen), so basic Japanese or pointing at photos is enough — no English menu or English-speaking staff is confirmed.

tokyo_jikasei_mensho_shibuya_p.gf_detail: The signature noodles are wheat-based dough with quinoa kneaded in to reduce carbohydrate/gluten content — sources describe this as "lower in gluten," explicitly not gluten-free. Not suitable for celiac disease or a strict gluten-free diet; cross-contamination in the shared kitchen (which also handles wheat-containing soy-sauce ramen) is not controlled for.
tokyo_jikasei_mensho_shibuya_p.vegan_detail: Four dedicated vegan ramen items are offered alongside the main (non-vegan) menu: vegan dandan noodles (with soup), vegan soupless (mazesoba-style) dandan noodles, vegan miso ramen, and spicy vegan miso ramen. These are prepared as fully plant-based bowls separate from the restaurant's chicken-paitan and A5-wagyu ramen, though made in the same shared kitchen. No source found explicitly detailing whether shared broth pots or hidden bonito/katsuo dashi are used elsewhere on the menu that could risk cross-contact for strict vegans concerned about shared equipment; ask staff if that matters to you.
tokyo_jikasei_mensho_shibuya_p.hours_raw: 11:00–23:00 daily (some secondary sources give slightly different weekday/weekend last-order times — 21:40 weekdays / 20:40 weekends — so confirm current hours before visiting, as this is a shopping-mall tenant).

chef_bio.specialty: For vegan diners: vegan dandan noodles (with or without soup) and vegan miso ramen (regular or spicy). The house's overall signature is chicken-paitan ramen topped with A5 Japanese wagyu.

anecdotes.text: The shop describes its vegan menu as part of a broader effort to make ramen enjoyable for guests with religious or allergy-related dietary restrictions, alongside stated interest in raising environmental awareness through ramen.
English-language reviewers highlight friendly, accommodating staff and a clearly marked vegan menu, describing it as a convenient stop near Shibuya Scramble for a warm, flavorful bowl.

vegan_cross_contact.text: Vegan dandan and vegan miso ramen are prepared in the same kitchen as the restaurant's chicken-paitan and A5-wagyu ramen.

staff_allergy_handling.text: Cross-contamination in the cooking environment cannot be guaranteed; guests with severe allergies are advised to confirm directly with the shop before ordering.

positives.text: English-language reviewers praise friendly, accommodating staff and a clearly marked vegan menu, calling it a convenient, warming stop near Shibuya Crossing.

tokyo_matsuou.gf_detail: The zaru soba is made namagona-uchi style with 100% buckwheat flour (no wheat binder in that noodle), which is unusual and noteworthy. However, this is a traditional, non-specialized soba shop: the dipping sauce (tsuyu) is soy-sauce based (soy sauce in Japan is typically wheat-containing unless stated otherwise), the shop also serves wheat-containing "kawari-soba" and tempura (wheat-flour batter) on the same menu, and there is no indication the noodles are boiled in separate water from any wheat-containing items or that a dedicated fryer is used. No allergen or celiac-specific information was found from the restaurant itself. Diners with celiac disease should ask staff directly about the tsuyu recipe and boiling/frying setup before ordering, and should not assume safety from the 100% buckwheat noodle alone.
tokyo_matsuou.vegan_detail: This is a traditional soba-and-tempura shop, not vegan-oriented. The dipping sauce (tsuyu) is dashi-based and almost certainly includes bonito (katsuobushi), and the tempura menu centers on live shrimp and conger eel. No plant-based dashi or vegan menu option was found in any source reviewed. A plain zaru soba with soy-based tsuyu might be closest to vegan-adjacent, but the bonito dashi would need to be confirmed or substituted by staff, which is unconfirmed.

chef_bio.origin: Founded in 1981 by owner Onodera, an independent-minded soba craftsman who set out to make soba unbound by the old guild techniques of the era.
chef_bio.background: 松翁 opened in Kanda Sarugakucho in 1981 as part of a new wave of independent, self-taught soba shops that broke from the established techniques of the old-line Edo soba lineages. Tucked a short walk from Jimbocho and Suidobashi stations, it became a favorite of local salarymen and soba enthusiasts, and count novelist Shotaro Ikenami among its regular patrons in his lifetime.
chef_bio.philosophy: A soba-zen approach that treats the meal as an unhurried sequence: soba-zakura small dishes and sake first, tempura fried and served one piece at a time, and the noodles eaten last so nothing arrives lukewarm.
chef_bio.specialty: Namagona-uchi zaru soba, hand-made with 100% buckwheat flour, and the shop's signature two-color "awase-mori" plate pairing a plain soba with a seasonal kawari-soba; tempura (shrimp and conger eel kept live in a tank by the entrance) is fried to order and brought to the table piece by piece.

anecdotes.text: Novelist Shotaro Ikenami, one of Japan's best-loved food-and-fiction writers, was a regular customer of the shop.
The shop keeps live shrimp and conger eel in a tank by the entrance and fries tempura to order, bringing each piece to the table as it's ready.

gf_cross_contamination.text: No restaurant-specific statement on separating gluten-free (100% buckwheat) noodle boiling water from wheat-containing noodles or tempura batter was found; this is a traditional soba shop without a specialized allergen protocol.

soy_sauce_wheat.text: No confirmation of a wheat-free (tamari) soy sauce; standard Japanese soy sauce used in soba tsuyu typically contains wheat.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The kitchen prepares shrimp and conger-eel tempura and bonito-based dashi alongside the soba, so cross-contact with animal products is likely for any vegan order.

positives.text: The zaru soba is made with 100% buckwheat flour (namagona-uchi), meaning the noodle itself, unlike standard nihachi soba, contains no wheat binder.

chef_bio.philosophy: The 'Journey' name reflects a concept of 'creating the self one wants to be': a space designed so vegan and non-vegan diners can share the same table and menu without compromise.

anecdotes.text: The founder has described being inspired to start AIN SOPH. after an experience during a tea ceremony, where the flavor of the tea evoked a sense of nature and the power of life, prompting the idea of a restaurant as 'a place to return to one's origin.'

gf_cross_contamination.text: AIN SOPH's kitchen is a shared space where wheat and non-wheat items are prepared together; it is not a dedicated allergen-free facility and the restaurant cannot guarantee that cross-contamination will not occur.

staff_allergy_handling.text: Gluten-free and other allergen items are clearly marked in English on the menu, but a diner who asked staff directly learned that some items labeled gluten-free actually shared a fryer with wheat items or used a non-gluten-free miso — confirming each dish individually with staff is recommended.

positives.text: Diners have praised the Shinjuku location for its convenient location and clearly available gluten-free options on the menu.

cultural_comfort.note: The restaurant runs an official English-language website and marks gluten-free/allergen items in English on the menu, making it easy for non-Japanese-speaking diners to navigate.

tokyo_tokyo_dominica.gf_detail: One independent blog post calls this shop's curry the "original gluten-free curry" (元祖グルテンフリーカレー), and like most Sapporo-style soup curry it is not thickened with the wheat-flour roux used in standard Japanese curry-rice sauce. However, this claim is not corroborated on the restaurant's own official materials, the soup is seasoned with a "Japanese-style dashi" that likely includes ordinary wheat-containing soy sauce, and several toppings (e.g., fried chicken) are typically flour-battered and cooked in a shared fryer with no confirmed dedicated gluten-free fryer or prep process. Treat any gluten-free claim as unverified — ask staff in detail about the specific soup base, seasoning, and toppings before ordering if you have celiac disease.
tokyo_tokyo_dominica.vegan_detail: No vegan menu, marking, or plant-based stock option was found in any source. The soup base is described by the restaurant as using a "Japanese-style dashi," which in standard Japanese cooking is typically bonito (fish) and/or kelp based — there is no indication this shop offers a fish-free alternative, so the curry is very unlikely to be vegan-safe as served. Vegans should assume the soup base contains fish-derived dashi unless staff confirm otherwise.

chef_bio.background: Tokyo Dominica opened its doors in Shinjuku on March 11, 2011 — the exact day of the Great East Japan Earthquake. With trains across Tokyo stopped and the city in chaos, almost no customers could reach the brand-new shop, but the staff kept going because they wanted people to taste their soup curry. The shop grew out of the founder's own experience: he had once eaten soup curry in Sapporo and was moved enough by it to bring the dish to Tokyo. The company later opened a sister shop, Yellow Spice, in Ginza in 2012, and another in Osaka in 2019.
chef_bio.philosophy: The kitchen builds its soup from dozens of spices simmered with a Japanese-style dashi stock, aiming for a curry that is easy to enjoy on a first bite but rewards repeat visits with its layered, evolving spice character — bringing Sapporo-style soup curry into everyday Japanese food culture rather than treating it as a novelty.
chef_bio.specialty: Build-your-own Sapporo-style soup curry: diners choose from five soup bases (yellow, black — with pork bone for richness, red — tomato and garlic, white — soy milk, and deep yellow — coconut milk), roughly twenty spice levels, and a wide range of toppings.

anecdotes.text: Tokyo Dominica opened in Shinjuku on the day of the 2011 Tohoku earthquake, when public transport across the city ground to a halt and the new shop had almost no customers on its first day — the staff pushed through the rocky start because they wanted people to taste their soup curry.
The shop's founder had eaten soup curry in Sapporo years earlier and was moved enough by the experience to open his own soup curry restaurant in Tokyo.

gf_cross_contamination.text: No dedicated gluten-free fryer or prep line is confirmed; fried toppings are likely cooked in shared equipment.

vegan_cross_contact.text: The restaurant describes its soup as built on dozens of spices plus a "wa-fu dashi" (Japanese-style stock); Japanese-style dashi is conventionally made with bonito flakes (katsuobushi) and/or kelp, and the restaurant does not state that a fish-free or plant-based stock option exists.

tokyo_yakuzen_hinabe_shinbasei.gf_detail: No gluten-free menu or allergen guide was found. This is a DIY hot pot restaurant: guests cook shared raw ingredients (vegetables, tofu, mushrooms, meat, noodles) in a communal pot and mix their own dipping sauce from a bar of 10+ condiments that includes soy sauce and oyster sauce — both typically wheat-containing in Japan — plus sesame paste and doubanjiang, all served with shared utensils. One of the four broth bases is a long-simmered chicken broth; the ingredient makeup of the other three (mala, mushroom, tomato) is not confirmed. Because sauces and pots are shared and self-served, cross-contact with wheat-based condiments is likely. Anyone needing a gluten-free meal should ask staff in detail before ordering.
tokyo_yakuzen_hinabe_shinbasei.vegan_detail: No vegan menu was found. The hot pot format lets guests choose vegetables, mushrooms, and tofu for their pot, but the shared self-serve sauce bar includes oyster sauce (not vegan), and one of the four confirmed broth bases is a chicken broth simmered over 10 hours; the mushroom and tomato broth bases' ingredients (whether they use meat/bonito-based stock) are not confirmed from available sources. Vegans should ask staff specifically about broth composition and avoid the chicken broth and oyster-sauce-based condiments.
tokyo_yakuzen_hinabe_shinbasei.notes: The restaurant specializes in yakuzen hot pot prepared by cooks trained in authentic Sichuan technique, built on the traditional Chinese idea of 医食同源 (food and medicine share the same root).

chef_bio.background: Before opening his own shop, the owner worked at the original インド富士 (India Fuji) curry restaurant in Higashi-Koganei. In February 2016 he opened インド富士子 (India Fujiko) as that restaurant's sister shop in Koenji, running an 8-seat counter that became a cult favorite among Tokyo curry enthusiasts. In October 2021 the shop relocated to Suidōbashi (Kanda-Sarugakucho, Chiyoda-ku), where it now runs a dual identity: a South Indian-style curry lunch counter by day under the name インド富士子, and an evening spice/izakaya bar called ムンド不二 (Mundo Fuji) by night.
chef_bio.philosophy: A personal, idiosyncratic take on South Indian cooking informed by firsthand experience of South Indian food culture, prized by curry devotees for depth and individuality rather than a standardized 'Indian restaurant' menu.
chef_bio.specialty: Lunch curry plate — choose 2 of the day's rotating curries (e. g. pork vindaloo, spinach chicken curry, fish curry, dal curry) served over basmati rice, ¥1,300

The owner was interviewed alongside musician Saya of Tenniscoats and Koiken of Atarashii Hito about the shop's identity and its move to Suidōbashi.

In an October 2023 social post marking two years at the Suidōbashi location, the owner wrote candidly that the shop had barely survived with supporters' help and was 'honestly about at its limit,' asking people to visit while it was still open.

chef_bio.background: Part of the 東京油組総本店 (Tokyo Abura Gumi Sohonten) abura-soba chain, which the operator's own promotional material traces to a long-established (multi-decade) noodle manufacturer that branched into running its own oil-noodle shops across Tokyo. This Shinjuku East Exit branch sits directly behind Studio Alta, tucked into a building with counter seating on the ground floor and further seating in the basement, and runs 24 hours a day so it doubles as a late-night/after-the-last-train option.
chef_bio.philosophy: The chain markets abura-soba as a lighter, lower-calorie alternative to broth ramen, built around the quality of the tare (sauce) and noodle rather than a long-simmered soup, with all bowl sizes (regular/large/extra-large) priced the same so portion size is the diner's choice.
chef_bio.specialty: 特製油そば (tokusei abura-soba) — thick, springy noodles tossed (not served in broth) with a proprietary blended soy-sauce tare, topped with menma, sliced pork chashu, negi and nori; a spicy miso version is also offered. Diners finish the bowl themselves with a few circles of vinegar and rayu chili oil, mixing before eating.

anecdotes.text: House description: the tare blends several different soy sauces to build depth of flavor under the oil-noodle format, with a separate spicy-miso tare balancing heat and miso richness.
Blog account of visiting the chain describes it as a specialty shop built around a rich soy-sauce tare finished tableside with vinegar and chili oil.

tokyo_tsurutontan_udon_noodle_.gf_detail: The udon here is traditional wheat-flour noodle, made fresh in-house at each location — there is no confirmed gluten-free noodle substitute for this restaurant in any source checked. The broth (kake-jiru) is soy-sauce based and soy sauce traditionally contains wheat. No dedicated gluten-free fryer or kitchen process was found. chef_bio.background: TsuruTonTan traces back to 1978, when Kato Seiichi — who grew up in the udon country of Sanuki, Kagawa — opened a hand-pulled udon shop called Honke Sanuki in Osaka, at a time when chewy, Sanuki-style udon wasn't common there. That shop's technique became the basis for TsuruTonTan, which opened in Osaka's Sōemonchō district in 1989, blending Sanuki noodle-making with Osaka's food culture. The brand is now run by Kato Pleasure Group and has grown into a chain across Osaka, Tokyo, and other cities, plus locations in the United States. The Shibuya Scramble Square branch opened in 2019 as the chain's seventh Tokyo location.
chef_bio.philosophy: Each restaurant makes its own noodles daily rather than using a central factory, aiming to serve udon at its peak just after boiling. The broth recipe — Hokkaido Rishiri kombu paired with Kagoshima Makurazaki bonito flakes — has reportedly stayed unchanged for more than three decades.

chef_bio.background: Iwase came to sushi relatively late, having started his culinary career at 21 after an earlier stint as a salaryman. He trained within the well-regarded "Sushi Sho" (すし匠) lineage of Edomae sushi restaurants, working at Sushi Sho Masa in Nishi-Azabu, Sushi Subaru in Aoyama, and Takumi Tatsuhiro in Shinjuku before striking out on his own in September 2012. The restaurant later relocated to its current Nishi-Shinjuku location near Tochomae Station in 2017.
chef_bio.philosophy: Food writers describe the restaurant's approach as "呑ます鮨" (sushi that makes you want to drink) — richly seasoned tsumami dishes interspersed with delicate nigiri, built around the rhythm of pairing food with sake rather than nigiri alone.
chef_bio.specialty: An alternating omakase of nigiri and otsumami (small savory side dishes) in the "Sushi Sho style," running to roughly 33-35 courses in total. Fish is sourced directly from the Yanagibashi Rengo Ichiba market in Hakata, Fukuoka, with Iwase reportedly traveling there himself to select seasonal seafood before it is shipped to the restaurant.

anecdotes.text: A restaurant reviewer describes Iwase's food as carrying on the Sushi Sho lineage in his own style, characterizing the meal as "呑ます鮨" because the richness of the otsumami keeps guests reaching for their sake cup between bites of nigiri.

Iwase trained through several branches of the Sushi Sho family of restaurants (Nishi-Azabu, Aoyama, Shinjuku) before opening his own counter in 2012, later moving to the current Nishi-Shinjuku address in 2017.

tokyo3__8.gf_detail: Not gluten-free and no GF options exist. Tokushima ramen at Todai is a wheat-noodle bowl in a rich soy-sauce-and-pork-bone (醤油とんこつ) broth — the broth is built on soy sauce, which is brewed with wheat, and the noodles are standard wheat chukamen. Signature toppings (simmered pork belly, seasoned menma, optional raw egg) sit in that wheat-soy broth, and diners are encouraged to add free rice, which does not change the wheat exposure. A celiac cannot safely eat here: wheat noodles + wheat-containing soy-sauce tare are unavoidable, and there is no dedicated GF preparation. Sources: tokushimakotomono.com review (describes it as 醤油とんこつベースのこってり系ラーメン, brown broth, pork belly, standard raw egg) and the official menu page.
tokyo3__8.vegan_detail: Not vegan or vegetarian. The core broth is pork-bone (とんこつ) simmered with soy sauce; the standard bowl is topped with simmered pork belly (豚バラ肉) and an optional free raw egg, both animal products. Even a plain bowl carries pork-bone dashi, so there is no hidden-dashi ambiguity to resolve — it is meat-based by design. No plant-based option is advertised.

chef_bio.background: 株式会社東大 (Todai Co., Ltd.) runs the Ramen Todai (ラーメン東大) chain, founded in Ōjin-chō, Tokushima City in April 1999, with the Daidō main store (大道本店) opening soon after. Per a Tokushima blog interview, the founder trained at the Tsuji Culinary Institute (辻調理師専門学校), apprenticed in Chinese restaurants at major hotels around Osaka Station, then worked at a large ramen chain before going independent in 1999; the surname 内藤 (Naitō) is cited for the president, but this is a single blog source and unconfirmed.
chef_bio.philosophy: The name 東大 was chosen to mean aiming for the very top (summit) of the ramen world — a play on the elite 'Todai' homonym expressing the ambition to reach the peak of ramen, not a link to Tokyo University. The company frames its mission as 'the evolution and cultural creation of Tokushima ramen' (徳島ラーメンの進化と文化創造).
chef_bio.specialty: Tokushima-style soy-tonkotsu ramen: a rich, dark brown soy-sauce-and-pork-bone broth with medium-thin noodles, sweet-savory simmered pork belly, seasoned menma, a free raw egg to crack in, and free rice on the side — the classic Tokushima 'ramen-with-rice' experience.

anecdotes.text: Won Grand Prix at the 2004 'Akashi Ramen Hatoba' event in Hyogo and the 2005 'Kuwana Ramen Kaidō' event in Mie, and took first place three years running (2005–2007) in the Tokushima town magazine Awawa's popular-ramen ranking.
A free raw egg cracked into the bowl is treated as standard for Tokushima ramen at Todai, and the shop leans into the local custom of eating the rich brown broth alongside white rice.

tokyo3__10.gf_detail: Treat as UNSAFE for a strict celiac unless verified in person. This is a traditional soba shop, and traditional soba is a high-gluten-risk cuisine in three independent ways: (1) Noodles — most Japanese soba is nihachi (二八, 80% buckwheat / 20% wheat) and is NOT gluten-free. Even where a shop offers juwari (十割, "100% buckwheat"), noodles are typically cut on a shared board dusted with wheat flour (uchiko) and boiled in the SAME pot of water used for wheat-containing soba/udon, so cross-contamination is routine. (2) Tsuyu/dipping sauce — standard soba tsuyu is made with regular soy sauce (shoyu), which contains wheat, so even a "gluten-free" noodle is served with a wheat sauce unless wheat-free tamari is specifically arranged. (3) Sides — tempura (ten-seiro, kakiage) uses wheat batter and is often fried in oil shared with the noodle kitchen. For reference, the same-named shop in Chiba lists its house "nami" soba at ~70% buckwheat (≈30% wheat) and its premium "ginbiraki" at 80–100% buckwheat with a nihachi new-soba in winter — i.e. its cheapest soba is decidedly not GF. A celiac should not rely on this entry; ask directly whether they cut a dedicated juwari with no wheat uchiko, boil it in fresh water, and can serve tamari-based tsuyu. Absent all three, answer is no.
tokyo3__10.vegan_detail: Not vegan by default. Traditional soba tsuyu (the hot broth and the cold dipping sauce) is built on katsuo dashi — dried bonito (fish) flakes, often plus mirin — so both hot kake-soba and cold zaru/mori-soba dipping sauce contain hidden fish. Kaiseki/set courses at such shops also commonly include egg (tamagoyaki, dashimaki), fish, and tempura seafood. Plain soba noodles with no sauce may be orderable, and some shops can make a kombu/shiitake (kelp/mushroom) dashi on request, but this must be confirmed — do not assume. Flag bonito dashi explicitly.
